label: Claude Opus 5.5
output:
**Thursday Afternoons on the Tea Trolley**

I should say at the outset that I am not a natural at this sort of thing. I spent 41 years as a bookkeeper, most of them at a builders' merchant in Dereham, and the most emotionally demanding part of my week was usually the VAT return. When I retired I assumed I would find plenty to do. I didn't, much. For about eighteen months I had no particular reason to leave the house on most days, and I drifted rather. Then in March 2022 a friend mentioned the tea trolley at Wensum Vale, and I thought I might as well.

My first Thursday I knocked an entire jug of milk over the trolley. Not a splash: the whole jug, across the cups, the saucers and a plate of custard creams. A patient called Pat laughed so hard she had to be handed a tissue, and when she'd recovered she told me it was the best afternoon she'd had in a month. I have been coming back ever since, though I like to think my pouring has improved.

I mention this because I suspect a good many of you who read this blog are fond of the hospice and might quite like to help, but assume that volunteering here must be either very harrowing or very skilled. On a Thursday afternoon in the day unit it is mostly neither.

The day therapy unit sees somewhere between 14 and 18 people on a Thursday. They come for the art group, for a hand massage, or simply for company, and most of them go home again afterwards. It is not a hushed, sad sort of place. It is noisy and rather jolly, with a good deal of chat and a fair bit of teasing. We go round with the trolley from half past one until four, pour tea, hand out biscuits and talk to whoever wants talking to.

You do not need any nursing skill. You need to be able to push a trolley, remember who takes what, and listen. I will admit that four decades of keeping ledgers straight has turned out to be handy for remembering who takes what. Mr Hollis, for instance, a retired signalman, takes two sugars, and every week he tells me about the 1953 floods, slightly differently each time. I have stopped correcting the dates. It isn't really about the dates.

You also learn the local customs. The bourbons always go first, without fail, so we now hide a packet for the late group. I'm not sure this is in any official guidance, but it works.

I won't pretend every week is easy. Some Thursdays are hard, and you will get to know people you then don't see again. When those days come, the staff look after us properly, and you are never left to muddle through on your own. But they are not most days, and I wouldn't want anyone put off by imagining that they are.

**Why I'm writing**

We have been two short since the summer. The Thursday rota is meant for six of us and at the moment there are four. One of our number moved to Sheffield to be near her grandchildren, which nobody could begrudge her, and another is recovering from a knee operation. The four of us are managing, but it would be a great deal better with six.

**What it involves**

The commitment is one Thursday afternoon a fortnight, 1.30 to 4pm. Bridget, our volunteer coordinator, does the induction herself. It takes about two hours, and you'll also do a short food hygiene course online, which the hospice pays for. That is genuinely all the training you need to start.

**Come and have a look**

There is a volunteer open afternoon on Tuesday 24 November at 2pm in the Willow Room. There will be tea and biscuits (bourbons, I'm told, if you're quick) and there is no obligation whatsoever. You can come, ask questions, have a cup of tea and go home again. I'll be there.

If you can't make that, ring Bridget on the volunteering line and she'll be glad to have a chat.

I'd very much like to see at least two new faces on the 24th. If you've been wondering whether you're the sort of person who could do this, I can tell you that I wondered the same, and then I spilled the milk, and it all turned out fine.
